en: Keened bitterly through the smoke.
Then the unfortunate Kanykey
Was mauled by the champions
And beaten by their warriors.
As they humiliated her,
They inflicted a terrible ordeal
Too dreadful for human eyes;
They committed such violence
As no living person could bear to witness.
Your poor, fierce-hearted mother,
Once upon a time,
In a time long past,
Had a proudly arching brow;
But when the hero’s eyes closed,
Her hope of seeing daylight grew faint.
The hair at her nape was like grass;
The ill fortune amid all her joys
Was too heavy for a camel to bear.
The hair at her nape stood stiff;
The ill fortune amid all her joys
Towered a spear’s height.
Kanykey moaned,
Sobbing like a camel for its calf.
“This is the khan’s decree,” they said,
And the forty champions who received the command
Rushed upon her like players fighting for the goat.
Her ribs and her poor waist,
In the champions’ hands,
Were crushed and shattered.
She had no strength left to cry “Ah,”
No sense left to answer “Yes”;
Your mother shrieked and wept.
Seeing it, the common folk—
The dear Argyn and Kyrgyz people—
Lamented and cried aloud.
When they saw your mother Kanykey,
The birches wept and the willows wept;
Every living soul who looked upon her wept,
Strong warriors wept,
And the murmuring multitude wept.
All who were weeping
Wept as though consumed by their own grief:
“Kanykey was his mother,
And Kanchoro was her son!
The ominous dream has come true;
Never in all the ages
Has a man so disgraced his mother!
What a black-hearted creature!
The people cannot endure such a khan.
He had his own mother dragged like the goat in kökbörü;
Now our strength is gone.
My dear, a villain who does this to his mother
Can never mount the throne again.
He brandishes and wheels his spear—
That black-hearted slave
Will utterly ruin the people.
He will surely unleash turmoil;
At the slightest move, he will
Slaughter all these people.
Sparing no one who stirs,
My dear, he will revel in massacre!
When that savage dog unleashes his assault,
He will slaughter
Everyone who so much as stirs.
He is a witless brute beyond measure;
A villain who treats his mother this way
Will spare no khan.
He will sow rebellion and begin strife,
And if he quarrels with
All these people, young and old,
He will surely destroy them.
And when madness seizes him again,
He will leave not one person alive
But slaughter them all.
He will scatter all the Kyrgyz;
My dear, if a dreadful enemy attacks with a war cry,
He will expose the Kyrgyz to ruin.
This accursed Kanchoro
Is wickedness itself,
The black eye of all strife.
He is a living torment;
Unable to find a worthy challenge, he ravages the land,
Unable to preserve them, he scatters and ruins the people.
He is no just soul fit to be khan;
Kanchoro is a witless fool,
No khan capable of ruling this nation.
Even his ordinary speech is venom;
He is not merely Kanchoro,
But truly the wrath of God.
He is a dark and dismal night,
One of those calamities
That destroy both nation and people.
His eyes are mottled and askew;
He is the very scourge of mankind.
His mischief and his vileness
Are enough for a host of men.
The lionlike sultan, the bloodthirsty hero,
Who did not take this swine’s head,
Crush him utterly, and finish him,
Was nevertheless a true-hearted man,
Of honest purpose and pure intent,
With sincerity in his breast.
This warrior, however, had always
Plotted treachery from the start;
Yet even when he wrecked everything entirely,
The noble prince, the heroic khan,
Never said, ‘He has ruined us.’”
So the people clamored,
But did they dare speak openly?
They talked in whispers
And stood clicking their tongues;
Wrathful words reached their ears,
But not one soul spoke in protest,
And every head bowed to the ground.
They tormented her frail life,
And the people wept at the sight of Kanykey.
The venerable lady blessed by fortune,
An exemplar to the mighty nation,
The precious legacy left to them
By our gray-maned father Manas,
Was a Night of Destiny for the Kyrgyz,
A sacred soul.
Her golden womb was a treasure;
She was the refuge
Of the dear Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
For the Kyrgyz here in Talas,
She was the black fruit upon the laden bough.
Ah, blessed noblewoman,
She was a whole nation to the multitude,
Rich as pure fat and choice suet,
A mother to all the people.
Look how a valley no multitude had trodden
Has become a common road;
Look how the mother of all the people
Has been brought to disgrace!”
The people wailed and grieved,
Their cries reaching God.
The dear people might have fought,
But had no strength to rescue her;
Each bowed his head to the ground.
The brave men among them
Could not bear to look upon your mother
And collapsed upon their sides.
The courageous lions among them
Looked upon your mother in anguish,
While all the remaining people
Fled in terror and scattered.
Khan Kanchoro began
His oppression and tyranny;
The people wailed and the nation panicked,
And a great many of those who remained
Abandoned all their livestock,
Renouncing everything they owned.
Kanchoro displayed his might
And unleashed his fiercest wrath;
The people trembled and the nation panicked,
And the Kyrgyz fled Talas,
Driven away by his fury.
Then Kanchoro
Issued an order to those beside him:
The madman summoned
All his wrestlers.
He began issuing orders:
“Do not let the buttocks
Of that raging old hag touch the ground.
Whenever you see her, stir up turmoil,
And grant her no great comfort.
In the morning, make the old woman
Chew and soften
Tough rawhide with her teeth!
At sunset, make the witch
Dance like the Kalmyks.
When night has passed and day returns,
Strap a waterskin upon her back,
Put a crooked staff in either hand,
And condemn the wretch to breaking stones.
Torment her like this,
Heap many hardships on the coward,
Find two barren yearling calves,
And prepare the place of her death;
Between those two barren calves
Bind her fast!
Do not kill her quickly,
But kill her through humiliation—
Thus finish off the infidel!
Among the horses are piebald chargers,
A mixed herd of Argyn and Kyrgyz stock.
When evening falls, this hag
Must not slip away unseen
And race about like a greyhound;
She must not keep disrupting the people.
At the black heart of the boiling spring,
Right beside the tall plane tree,
Dig a great dungeon forty ropes deep
And make a place there;
When evening falls, cast the old woman
Into that pit!
By day, drag the old woman
From the pit and make her ready;
To the two barren calves
Bind her tightly by the waist!
Bind her fast and secure,
And across the paths she might walk
Dig deep, broad trenches;
Make the infidel suffer
Every torment under heaven!”
So Kanchoro spoke,
And when he commanded, the forty wrestlers—
Who cut off heads when told to take a cap,
Who spilled their very souls when told to spill blood,
Who drank poison when told to drink water—
All forty wrestlers,
Stronger than ordinary men,
With their precious swords,
Like men struck by slaughter,
At the sound of Kanchoro’s voice
All fell upon their task.
They never failed to do his bidding:
To the two barren calves
They bound her tightly by the waist.
While they abused your mother,
While they heaped misery upon her,
Before he had even finished speaking,
Before anyone could say another word,
Külchoro’s wife Akbala
Came running in anguish,
With the white dagger bought
For sixty camels and forty colts
Drawn ready from its sheath,
Praying to the spirit
Of her forefather who had passed into eternity.
She was the finest of women,
The daughter of Jamgyrchy,
One set apart from other mortals—
That wife of Külchoro.
She had heard a tale from a gossip,
Heard that her revered old mother
Had been savagely mauled,
Heard that Chürök had been taken as spoil
And subjected to humiliation,
Heard that in her old age Kanykey,
Your mother, had been stripped of dignity
And cruelly oppressed.
Wailing aloud, Akbala
Plunged into mortal peril;
The poor woman cast aside
Her fragile life, believing herself already dead.
Her knees bent toward the ground,
She ran on, wailing aloud,
As though her ribs were breaking apart;
Grievous torment and certain death
Appeared before the doomed woman.
Immeasurably swift,
The ill-fated woman sped on;
With no care for her fragile life,
Broad-rumped, with wide-swinging braids,
